transcript_data.text: In the past couple hundred years, we’ve called a lot of things the November Revolution. As far back as the 1830s, when Poland rebelled against the Russians.
You had the famous October Socialist revolution that technically took place in November if you use the Gregorian calendar.
You then have the creation of the Weimar Republic in Germany following World War 1, and most
recently we had the 1989 Velvet revolution which ended the communist rule in Czechoslovakia,
the same month that the Berlin Wall fell. But I’m here to talk about November of 1974.
The United States is coming to terms with the resignation of Richard Nixon just a few months prior.
The midterm elections of 1974, under Gerald Ford, were a slaughter for Republicans.
Democrats stole an astonishing 49 seats, securing the 2/3rds majority that would allow them to override Ford’s presidential veto powers.
In the nearly 50 years since it remains the largest net gain of seats for the Democratic
party. But no one calls this the November Revolution of 1974. That name belongs to a decidedly non-political event.
Physics is about to experience a coincidence so remarkable, so improbable, that we’re
unlikely to see anything like it ever again. By this point most of the physics community was in agreement that atoms were made up of
three things. A dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by a fuzzy cloud of electrons.
And all the observable matter in the universe was just combinations of these three ingredients.
But by the 1960s, there were those who suspected that maybe there was a level even deeper than
the subatomic. An even smaller set of particles that made up the protons and neutrons.
Quarks, as they were called, supposedly came in three flavours: Up, down and strange.
And despite some experimental evidence in favour of this quark model, it was still up for debate whether quarks were actual physical particles, or just useful mathematical concepts
that helped to resolve some of the weirdness of certain experiments. Sure, they fixed a few problems here or there, but they seemed like a band-aid applied to
what was a huge whole in the jigsaw puzzle. But this attitude would change thanks to an unexpected result off the California coast.
Burton Richter was leading a team at Stanford, working on their newest $6 million toy.
A tunnel loop 80 meters in diameter known as SPEAR.
This is a very expensive tunnel in which electrons and their antimatter equivalents are rammed
together at high speeds in the hope that they’ll explode into new particles. As is typical in physics when a breakthrough is made, everyone assumed that something must
be broken, because they weren’t even looking for a new particle. And yet there it was, flashing into existence for just seven zeptoseconds, with an energy
of 3 billion electron volts. This wasn’t evidence of the up, down or even strange quark.
This was something new. This was a 4th quark. Specifically, a 4th quark appearing in tandem with its antimatter equivalent, before they
annihilate each other. Now a 4th quark had been proposed before, but never seen in the wild.
If this was truly the 4th quark, charm as its now called, the band-aid could come off.
They had just found the missing jigsaw piece. Richter had wanted to name the hybrid particle SP, after the accelerator that had discovered
it, but his coworkers didn’t like that name. So instead, he asked a Greek colleague which Greek letters were still available.
Iota was free, but he opted against it since iota is a synonym for insignificant, which
felt counterintuitive to the magnitude of this discovery. So in the end he settled on Psi.
Later they would observe the path that the particle took using a spark chamber. A spark chamber is a stack of high voltage metal plates filled with helium and neon.
When a high energy particle passes through it, the gas ionizes, leaving a trail of visible sparks.
And somehow, the spark trail was the exact shape of the letter psi.
Now, this fact on its own, is crazy. That a particle was named, and very soon after, resembled the shape of its name.
But this wasn’t the coincidence I mentioned earlier. That exact same month, on the opposite side of the country, a group is working out of
Brookhaven National Laboratory on Long Island. Leading the team was Samuel Ting, and with their own collider, the larger and more powerful
AGS, they had stumbled onto the exact same charm-anticharm particle. Ting called the particle J. As the story he goes he chose J because it’s remarkably
similar to the Chinese character in his own name. Other stories behind the name have cropped up over the years.
But if I had to choose a personal favourite story, it’s that J is the first letter of his daughter’s name.
On the 11th of November, Ting flew to Stanford for unrelated reasons, and just happened to
cross paths with Richter. When both men excitedly told the other about their recent breakthroughs, they soon realized
there were talking about the same thing. Later that day they jointly announced the discovery of J/Psi.
It’s astounding that such an important discovery was made independently within such a short
period of time. For this reason J/Psi is the only subatomic particle that has two officially recognized
names. But we don’t call it the November Revolution because of one discovery. We call it that because it pointed the whole field in a specific direction, kicking off
a decade of discoveries. That same year, Jean Iliopoulos would compile what is now widely understood to be the first
ever edition of the standard model of physics. At this point it’s a jigsaw puzzle still missing some critical pieces.
And you know how jigsaws are. Even if a piece is missing you can still kind of infer what it should look like.
Maybe you recognize some of the names here: This outer ring we call the Fermions, AKA the matter particles.
The top half is the family of quarks, note that you’ll never find one of these on their own, only in larger combinations called hadrons.
Only three years after the discovery of charm, the first evidence of an even heavier fifth quark was found.
This new one was named the bottom quark. What this suggested was that a sixth partner quark was also out there, waiting to be found.
And thus the search for the massive, but elusive, top quark had begun. Gotta tell ya, this is one hell of a naming convention.
On the other side here we have the leptons. Unlike quarks you can actually find these alone in the wild.
They consist of the electron, who you may recognize from their greatest hit: electricity.
Less well known are its big sibling the muon, and the even more recently discovered even bigger sibling, tau.
Each of these three have their own corresponding pets, the neutrinos. One of them is still just implied, but we're pretty sure it's out there.
Moving on inward we have another class of particles, the bosons. If fermions make up matter because they’re *firm*, then bosons make up the four fundamental
forces...I don’t have a mnemonic for this one. The photon you’ve probably heard of, it’s responsible all light and EM waves.
You can thank Einstein for that one. At the tail end of the 1970s the gluon had popped up in experiments, it’s responsible
for gluing together quarks to make protons and neutrons. The other two here are still missing in action.
You have the W and Z bosons, which supposedly control nuclear radiation and decay.
Their existence was so certain though, that theoretical work suggesting them had already won a Nobel prize.
And that’s about all there is to it! Well, no, not *technically*.
There were those who proposed another boson, one that would tie all the other particles
together in a field, and this field would explain the origin of mass.
At this point it was not so widely accepted, and thus its time in the spotlight will come much later.
So, as the 1970s gave way the 1980s, this was the state of the standard model and most
of particle physics. But something was becoming clear. To make further progress, and find those missing pieces, the technology needed to catch up
first. The heavier the particle, the higher the energy needed to produce it. They needed bigger accelerators.
And thus 14 years after their first joint announcement, Burton Richter and Samuel Ting
would be reunited. Not for the first time, they had after all jointly accepted a Nobel prize some years
back. And yet, despite the prestige of the Nobel ceremony, this occasion was no less monumental.
A few feet away from them, the announcement is being made for what will be the largest scientific undertaking in United States history.
It would be the particle physics equivalent of landing on the moon. Their mission, was to find the holy grail of particle physics.
And Ronald Reagan was all in. "Outer space used to be called the final frontier.
But today we've begun to tap another frontier: Inner space, whose infinitesimal constellations
hold out infinite possibilities. I know that some people may question the practical applications of the superconducting super
collider. But the truth is, the practical applications of this knowledge are already changing the
way we live. In the face of ever increasing global competition, the United States must maintain the leading
edge in science and technology, and building the world's largest particle accelerator is
a visible symbol of our nation's determination to stay out front. " Within 5 years the project will have completely collapsed.
And with it, American leadership in the realm of particle physics. Burton Richter would go on to call the project “one of high energy physics’ greatest
failures”. I’m warning you now. This story has a lot of things.
What it doesn’t have, is a happy ending. This was a failure so big, so massive in its scope, that it's hard to put into words.
Instead, I think it's better if I let you see for yourself.
If I gave you a rock, and asked you to describe what the inside of it looked like, with no
access to fancy tools, what would you do? Personally, I’d throw it at the ground repeatedly until it broke.
At some point humans realized that the best way to find out what something is made of, is to smash it open.
And if it’s a rock or an apple, our hands can get the job done. But if we wanted to break apart something small, like say, a proton?
We’re gonna need some specialized gear. Hence, particle accelerators. A particle accelerator, but more specifically, a collider, consists of three main components.
1. A tunnel system. Generally a circular loop, that is held at vacuum, and at temperatures close to absolute
zero. This is what the particles will be travelling through. 2. A set of ultra-strong magnets.
These serve two purposes. Most of the ring is surrounded by equally spaced magnets, and their job is to steer
the charged particles around the ring. Additionally, you have a specific region where the magnets are used to speed up the particles
once every loop. Like a booster in Mario Kart. After thousands of loops per second, the particles have approached the speed of light.
And finally 3. The collision zone, this region usually contains an advanced detector that gathers hundreds
of gigabytes of data per second. Think blood splatter analysis, only real.
Modern accelerators are typically built in several stages. With linear injecting segments, multiple booster sections, etc.
Like the incremental stages of a rocket. But by and large, accelerators are just big guns we build underground, and we use them
to get really really tiny bullets to ram into each other and explode.
Why? Because collisions release a ton of energy, and energy is related to mass through Einstein’s
iconic equation: E = mc^2. So, if you want to generate heavier quarks, we need larger energies, and larger machines.
And for the past two decades, one nation has been the undisputed world champion when it
comes to building accelerators. Throughout the 60s and 70s, 5 quarks and 2 leptons were discovered in the United States.
The fruits of the November Revolution. At the turn of the 1980s, the US was operating 4 major accelerator labs.
You had SLAC, over in California where we met our buddy Richter, and you had Brookhaven in New York with our buddy Ting, as well as Cornell a little ways away in Ithaca.
But the newest and shiniest, was the crown jewel of the America’s particle accelerators,
the Tevatron, located at Fermilab in the outskirts of the Windy City of Chicago.
The Tevatron name is an amalgamation of two things: 1. TeV is short for tera-electron volts, or a trillion electron volts.
That’s the approximate collision energy the machine is capable of generating. And the other half, tron, because it’s funny to name expensive scientific instruments with
the suffix tron. With a loop diameter of 2 km and state of the art superconducting magnets, the Tevatron
was the worlds first collider to break the energy barrier from GeV to TeV.
That was the true final frontier. As the standard model began to get filled in, the missing puzzle pieces were beginning
to take shape. That meant the top quark, the W and Z bosons, and maybe, just maybe, the Higgs boson.
The United States, and its highly decorated army of physicists, wanted to be the ones to plant down that flag.
Bring home that W. Now consider how many accelerators existed in the rest of the world. In Western Europe you had CERN, straddling the French and Swiss borders, and DESY in
Germany. The Soviet Union had two accelerators all to themselves. And finally, the rookies on the scene, you had Japan, with their KEK accelerator lab.
(I swear that is the actual name). You may have noticed here, that the US has almost half the world’s major accelerators.
And for a while that was a major strength of the Americans. But as the 1980s rolled around, this was turning into a weakness.
See, the US budget for particle physics had to be split between 4 labs that varied in
size, age, and capabilities. To keep each of them competitive would require multiple ongoing upgrades that would spread
the slim budget even slimmer. The fear was that Europe’s consolidation into one entity, CERN, would allow them to
take the lead. CERN was already digging a tunnel for its newest collider, the large electron-positron
collider, or LEP. With a diameter of 8.6 km, it would be by far the world’s largest, making Fermilab’s
2 km look quaint. To maintain their competitive edge, US physicists would have to 1-up CERN.
Instead of 4 small labs competing for funding, the path forward should be a new giant lab.
All the eggs in one basket. Throughout the 70s there were conferences held over and over again, with dreams of a
VBA. Or, very-big-accelerator. That name was coined by Leon Lederman, then the director of Fermilab, and the leader of
the team that had discovered the bottom quark. Generally considered the godfather of this hypothetical new accelerator, he would be
the project’s biggest cheerleader in the years to come. But concrete plans wouldn’t materialize until 1982, at a conference in Snowmass Colorado.
Lederman again led the charge, calling for a new gargantuan American collider that would be able to support energies as high as 40 TeV, with a loop diameter of 30 km or higher.
This was an absurdly high energy and a massive footprint to go along with it, and thus would
require an enormous location to build it. Something flat and empty. The hypothetical machine was therefore nicknamed the Desertron.
A year later in 1983, CERN announced the discovery of the W and Z bosons.
There were no buts about it, Europe had taken the lead in the boson race. With the pressure mounting even further, a government sponsored panel was organized,
and the American project got its official name. The SSC, or: The Superconducting Super collider.
A machine so grand and ostentatious, its name included the word ‘super’ twice.
Rough estimates pegged the cost of such a machine at somewhere between 4-8 billion, going by 2021 US dollars.
Now look, I get that 1 billion is a big number, so big that it’s basically meaningless without
a reference frame. So I've assembled a few comparisons. The taller the height, the more expensive it is.
We have the most expensive skyscraper ever built at $4 billion. The most expensive stadium ever built, at $5.5 billion.
And also the most expensive bridge at $7.5 billion. For a little mobile flavour the most expensive plane is the B2 stealth bomber at $2.43 billion,
and the most expensive ship ever built was the USS Gerald R. Ford at $13 billion.
For some scientific comparisons we have the Mars Rover at a humble $2.725 billion, the
Human Genome project at $5 billion, GPS satellites at $12 billion, and the Hubble Telescope coming
in at a hefty $13.5 billion. What about one of the largest American engineering projects of the 20th century, the Panama canal?
$19.7 billion. So overall, I don’t think we’re doing too bad considering this thing may or may
not unlock the secrets of the universe. But still, there was only one way they were going to pay for a machine that expensive.
The American taxpayer. And to be clear, each of America’s previous big 4 colliders were paid for the same way!
But each of these had a comparatively baby budget of a few hundred million dollars. Look at em!
Little baby machines. Don’t get me wrong, that’s nothing to scoff at, that's a lot of money. But when it comes to taxpayer funded projects, there’s a big difference in a price tag
that starts with an ‘m’ vs a price tag that starts with a ‘b’. Not only that, these 4 colliders were built during a period of American history that was
far more sympathetic to the whims of physicists. How do I put this…? Ever since they dropped the bomb on Hiroshima, the United States had supplanted itself ahead
of Europe to become one of two global superpowers. And, again, partially thanks to that very same atom bomb, America took the lead in another
area: Nuclear physics. Since world war 2, nuclear and particle physicists have enjoyed a certain amount of privilege
not afforded to other subfields in physics. With the successful completion of the Manhattan project, which btw, clocked in at around $30
billion in today’s money, it seemed only logical to create an organization would manage any future research into nuclear weapons…I mean nuclear energy.
That led to the creation of the Atomic Energy Commission, or AEC. It was a confidential agency that had the luxury of operating largely out of the public
eye, only having to answer to the Congressional committee on Atomic Energy, at meetings that were always held behind closed doors.
For the most part, nuclear physicists were given blank cheques to build powerful nuclear reactors and colliders on the pretense that their research was advancing national security.
And particle physicists fell into two camps over this. On the one hand you had the war hawks, people like Edward Teller and Harold Agnew who actively
championed the defense applications of nuclear research and were more than happy to enjoy the money they were showered with.
And on the other hand, you had the physicists who didn’t much care for the war and weapons
of mass destruction things, but were willing to look the other way if it meant getting the funding they required for their real passions.
It’s how the sausage got made, and no one was about to bite the hand that fed them. But this age of scientific free reign was about to change.
The anti-war and anti-nuclear movement of the 60s led to harsh criticism of the AEC.
It neglected radiation protections, reactor safety, and had a laissez faire attitude when it came to environmental pollution.
Congress was so fed up with the lack of oversight that they voted to abolish the AEC in 1974.
The 1970s as a whole were a time of dramatic upheaval for America. It had been rocked by the Watergate scandal, and America’s dominance in the automobile
and electronics industries was waning, leading to Europe and Japan taking over. This, combined with unrest in the Middle-East had led to a global oil crisis, rampant inflation,
and a massive recession. In response to this, President Jimmy Carter created a new department in 1977: The Department
of Energy, the DOE. The DOE was organized to manage and fund research into a variety programs, such as solar power,
renewables, synthetic fuels, etc. Additionally, all nuclear responsibilities, peaceful or otherwise, were absorbed into
the newly created department. No longer would their funding be automatically rubber-stamped, the DOE would be subject to
the whims of congress and the *public* subcommittee on Energy and Water Projects.
The age of the nuclear physicists always getting what they wanted was over. They’d have to compete for funding like every other subfield.
So as a first tentative step, the DOE approved a meager $52 million to begin R&D in 1984.
But if the SSC was going to turn that ‘m’, into a ‘b’, they had to get some key people in Washington on board.
They had to make a deal with the devil.
The SSC only got off the ground due to an alliance of convenience. There had never before been a scientific project of this scope, both in physical size and financial
cost. Unlike previous American accelerators funded by the US government, this was going to be the first to cross the billion dollar threshold.
In fact it was projected to cross it a dozen times. And as a consequence, it was not going to be able to quietly funded without significant
public scrutiny. In particular, it needed the stamp of approval of one very specific person.
There are two Ronald Reagan quotes often associated with the SSC, both of which came following
a cabinet meeting on January 29th of 1987. At the end, when Reagan finally gave his approval for the project, he was told that his decision
would make “a lot of physicists ecstatic.” His reply was “That’s probably fair, because I made two physics teachers in high school
very miserable”. But the other quote gives a little more insight into Reagan’s thought process.
Following a presentation on the merits of funding the project, he reportedly pulled out an index card from his jacket pocket, and went on to recite a poem by Jack London.
“I would rather be ashes than dust.” This continued for about a minute. In a moment that is very on-brand for late-stage Reagan, those in the room with him were unclear
what he was trying to say. Reagan would clarify with a different quote, which he pulled from his days spent as a football
announcer. He was telling physicists to “throw deep”. It was time for a Hail Mary.
It may be surprising to you that Ronald Reagan of all people, would be so enthusiastic about
a multi-billion dollar project that is incredibly abstract and with almost no short term economic
or strategic benefits. But I think the line “throw deep” perfectly encapsulates Ronald Reagan’s distinct brand
of cold war posturing. It took nearly 6 years of delicate political maneuvering by physicists and bureaucrats
alike to get Reagan to throw deep with the SSC and the Department of Energy. It was like playing political whack-a-mole, every time physicists would gain one ally
in Washington, they’d either retire or get promoted, only to be replaced by someone who wasn’t a fan of the project.
But eventually, they’d managed to sway several key members around the big man himself. First was George Keyworth, a nuclear physicist serving as Reagan’s first science advisor.
Eventually he was joined by Alvin Trivelpiece, director of energy research at the DOE. He did a lot of leg-work to eventually get the support of John Herrington, Secretary
of Energy. And Herrington was finally high enough up the bureaucratic food chain to arrange that fateful cabinet meeting, where Trivelpiece gave the pitch that ultimately swayed Reagan.
All of this is especially remarkable, given that when Reagan first took office in 1981,
one of his first acts was to try and shut the DoE down. During his presidential campaign Reagan had actively made promises to do just that.
The department was the exact kind of red-tape, big government overreach he villainized through his politics.
As soon as he took office Reagan slashed programs left and right and began to dismantle the department.
He cut all funding to all the renewable energy and synthetic fuel. In a particularly spiteful and performative act, he removed the solar panels Carter has
installed on the White House roof. You can see just how little Reagan cared about the department by looking at who he chose
to run it. Throughout Reagan’s 8 years in office he would appoint 3 secretaries of Energy, each of whom was uniquely unqualified.
His first pick was a dentist-turned politician. His next choice, Donald Hodel was closer, as an ex power grid administrator.
And yet he’s most remembered for his proposed solution to the hole in the ozone layer, which was not to try and fix it, but rather suggesting that everyone just wear hats and sunscreen.
His final Secretary was John Herrington, a California Real Estate developer, perfect.
Now, hindsight has painted Reagan as anti-science. But I think this is a misconception.
Reagan could be pro science. After some small cuts in his first year in office, there was an immediate reversal, funding
for federal research & development grew by a whopping 50%. But of course…this came with a big fat asterisk.
Reagan was funding a very specific type of science. As you might be aware, the Department of Energy is still around today, Reagan never went through
with completely gutting it. And it’s likely because once he took office, he realized the department’s true purpose.
The DOE handles the country’s nukes. So of course, under Reagan, while almost everything in the DoE was cut, the nuclear energy, and
the nuclear weapons programs received massive increases. But let’s visualize this in another way. You see those mountains back there?
Well, they aren’t actually mountains, they’re the annual United States military budget.
Now obviously this is on a different vertical scale than our collider here. If I put them on the same scale everything would be so squashed as to be useless.
It's mostly for the aesthetic, but also to give you a sense of the evolving priorities of the US government.
The Reagan bump, or Mount Gipper as I like to call it, is staggering when compared to
the administrations that came immediately before and after it. Reagan oversaw the largest peacetime buildup in US military history.
Reagan was intent on winning the cold war, and his strategy was to outspend the Soviets in every area they could.
And while most of this new funding was going towards personnel and equipment, an ever increasing
amount of it was going towards creating a new generation of high tech weapon systems. Before Reagan, if you broke down all R&D funding in term of civilian and military, military
comes in at just 47%. Under Reagan those digits just straight up swapped, up to a whopping 74%.
Three quarters of all R&D funding was now being used exclusively for military purposes.
Take it from Reagan’s science advisor, George Keyworth: “those areas that are most exciting and those most necessary to the economy or national defense should be supported at a
higher level than areas that are dormant”. Thankfully, for particle physicists, there was an upside.
One of the ‘exciting’ areas Keyworth was referring to was the search for the W and Z bosons over in Europe.
Despite Reagan’s priorities being defense, he was also a firm believer that the government had the responsibility to fund basic research, that meant low-level physics and chemistry.
Recognizing that even though there were no short term applications, many years down the line the research would prove to be essential.
For that reason, and the influence of Alvin Trivelpiece, funding for the office of energy research rose by 80% under Reagan.
If a few Americans could win some Nobel prizes, then hey, that’d be a nice bonus.
Other fields of science were not so lucky, and they began to resent nuclear physics as the teacher’s pet of the US government.
Less flashy areas such as condensed matter physics, renewable energy, medicine, saw their budgets stagnate due to inflation, or in the worst cases, receive deep cuts.
In the eyes of the Reagan admin they were too application heavy, those areas should be the responsibility of private industry, the invisible hand of the glorious free market.
And of course, you can’t discuss Reagan underfunding science without addressing his callous indifference to the AIDS crisis, which lead to millions of unnecessary deaths.
After years of protests and criticism from gay rights activists and epidemiologists, Reagan would reluctantly appoint a commission to deal with the AIDS crisis in 1987.
Of course, in a very Reagan move, he selected Admiral James D. Watkins to be in charge of
the committee. Once top dog of the navy, his appointment was widely criticized, and questioned even
by Watkins himself. He was after all, a devout Catholic who supported the military's ban on gay service members.
Despite what you might expect, Watkins took his job seriously, advocating for $50 million
in funding for research, improved sexual health education, and he criticized religious bigots who considered the disease an act of god.
In his commission report he would go on to request anti-discrimination laws for those suffering from AIDS.
The commission report passed by a slim vote of 7-to-6. Reagan would go on to ignore most of the suggestions made by Watkins.
Although he didn’t say so publicly, behind the scenes Watkins was said to have been angered and depressed.
But there was only one thing that Reagan loved more than the amount he hated the gaze.
Space. Throughout the 80s, NASA’s budget was either stagnant, or marginally declining.
But in actuality, Reagan was pumping plenty of money into space tech. It was just going to a different department.
The department of defense. See NASA is explicitly for non-military space applications.
Military space funding simply falls under the classified umbrella of the Air force, and its space division far outpaced the budget of NASA.
When it came to space projects, Reagan had a knack for betting on overambitious ideas that hemorrhaged money, and never saw the light of day.
For example, during Reagan’s 1984 state of the union address, where he said the words free and freedom 25 times, he announced that he was directing NASA to build the ludicrously
named Space Station Freedom. This bloated project was intended to be a peaceful civilian-based orbiting research
lab until the Department of Defense began encroaching, demanding that it could at any
point, carry out national security work on the station, unvetted and without the permission of any of the other nations sharing the station.
Indeed, any partner nations would not be allowed to “displace either the reality or symbol
of US leadership”. Would it surprise you that other nations were reluctant to join onto the project?
Ultimately the bloated plan was never able to get off the ground, underwent nearly 7 redesigns and scale-backs, before ultimately being scrapped in 1993.
Another of these pipe-dreams was the so-called Orient Express Space Plane, a hypersonic plane
that could take off and land at regular airports, but which could also deliver satellites into space.
After spending around $3 billion, the project was canned in 1994, and the technology was considered unworkable.
But of all of Reagan’s failed cold war babies, the most ridiculous of all of these was an
outer space, laser-based missile defense system that was nicknamed Star Wars.
It never saw the light of day because it relied on magical X-ray laser technology that hadn’t
been invented yet. It still, hasn’t been invented yet! The missile defense system was pure science fiction, but Reagan was so enamored with the
idea that his obsession killed the 1986 nuclear disarmament talks with Gorbachev.
Ronnie loved his sci-fi space laser so much that he walked away from what would have been the effective end of the cold war.
Throughout its life-cycle Star Wars wasted nearly $60 billion over 10 years before being
scrapped completely. But to hear it from Reagan’s top generals, these colossal wastes of money weren’t entirely
wastes of time. See, these lofty science fiction projects may have been unattainable in hindsight, but
so long as the USSR thought they were even remotely possible, the Soviets would continue to sink billions of dollars they didn’t have into trying to keep pace with the Americans,
hopefully one day bankrupting them. And to a certain extent, money troubles did lead to the collapse of the Soviet Union.
But on the other hand, this relentless defense build-up led to a massive deficit that would follow the US into the next two administrations.
So with all this context, it should be obvious now why Reagan was so eager to support the SSC.
George Keyworth knew that Reagan had a personal investment in projects that appeared imaginative and ambitious, and thus worked hard to pitch the SSC in the same light as projects like
Star Wars. But whereas those projects helped probe the frontier of outer space, the SSC would probe
the opposite end of the spectrum: Inner space. And when I use the term frontier, that’s not me clumsily adding subtext, it was the
specific language used by many physicists to help sell the SSC as a way to reassert
American dominance. To give you a sense of how the government viewed the SSC, Secretary Herrington stated
that the SSC would be the high energy physics equivalent of “putting a man on the moon”. And in a lot of ways the SSC truly was like putting a man on the moon.
For one, the US did not win the space race, let's get that out of the way. They were beaten by the Soviet Union to every conceivable milestone.]
It was only by choosing a grand and ostentatious goal with a high chance of failure, was the US able to move the goalposts, and reshape the narrative that they won the space race.
This was an approach typical of US government funded science. Bold big advancements, where they would leapfrog over the competition.
And whereas they competed with the Soviet Union when it came to space, their rival in the realm of particle physics was Western Europe.
American projects aimed for the stars, designing riskier, bigger machines that were miles ahead of the slower, less ambitious and meticulously engineered European counterparts.
Europe’s accelerators were far more likely to work on their first attempt, but that slower process meant that throughout the 60s and 70s, the US had beat them to many important
breakthroughs. The SSC was very much following this template, a bold leap forward in terms of both max energy
and size. But it was also very risky, years of R&D would be required for magnets, a massive empty location
with stable geology that could handle years of tunneling. It was a massive gamble, but it was the kind of gamble that Reagan loved to make.
In 1987, in a last ditch effort, the director of CERN, Herwig Schopper, testified in front
of congress, and argued that the US should abandon the SSC and join up with Europe.

Even better, they were specifically making the tunnels large enough so that if they wanted to upgrade it 10 years down the line, to an even stronger collider, that option would

Meet Maury Tigner. Maury has been toiling away in the background of the story for a while now. When the DOE approved an initial research phase for the SSC in 1984, Maury was picked
to lead the planning team out of Berkeley California. He was widely viewed among the community as one of the brightest minds in accelerator
design, having been responsible for Cornell’s accelerator. The DOE was impressed with Tigner’s efficiency and thoroughness, and also by how he inspired
loyalty in his team. He worked hard and his team respected him. And in a field with so many conflicted voices, the DOE viewed him as the only suitable candidate
to become the full-time leader of the R&D. With the plan laid out, the DOE allocated a few dozen million in funding, a small enough
amount that congress didn’t have to be consulted. Like I mentioned previously, accelerators are really just three components.
A tunnel system, thousands of ultra strong magnets, and a series of detectors. The detectors thankfully could come much later in the project’s life.
The key criteria that needed to be figured out were A. How big is the tunnel loop going to be, and B. How were they going to make the magnets?
Collider performance is really a three-way compromise between the size, max energy, and
magnet strength. Ideally we’d make the loop as small as we could, because tunneling and construction is incredibly expensive.
But at the same time, if we want a smaller loop, we need stronger magnets, and magnets
aren’t cheap either. And these weren’t just any magnets, they were going to be 17 meter-long superconducting
Niobium-Titanium magnets, which meant that to maximize their performance, they would need to be held at temperatures barely above absolute zero.
If they rise in temperature too much, just 4.35 degrees above absolute zero, the magnets quench and lose their superconductivity.
This is usually followed by a rapid surge of heat that can melt components, or even cause an explosion.
For all these reasons, each magnet would likely cost around tens of thousands of dollars, and they’d need nearly around 8000 of them.
So to summarize: If you lock-in max energy and lock-in magnet strength, the size of the
collider is really the only variable they could increase. Somewhere in the middle of all this was the sweetspot, and Maury Tigner’s team needed
to find it. Early in 1984, there were reports from CERN that evidence of the top quark had been found.
This turned out to be not the case, but the false alarm still put pressure on the design team. CERN kept bragging that their eventual upgrade could support energies up to 18 TeV, the SSC
needed to go above and beyond that to justify its existence. So for both technical and political reasons, Tigner’s group decided on a colossal total
energy of 40 TeV. The loop would have a diameter of 30 km, nearly 3 times as big as CERN’s.
If predictions were correct, the SSC would absolutely find the top quark, and hopefully,
the Higgs boson as well. They estimated a 9 year project length, 3 for full R&D, and 6 for construction.
The new estimate for costs was updated to $7.5-8.3 billion, on the higher end but certainly
not outrageous. After soliciting a number of different magnet proposals that varied in shape, materials
and strength, they settled on a magnet that could operate at 6.6 T, powered by nearly
12,000 Amps of current. This magnet won out over a design by a group from Texas, who had a cheaper, but weaker
magnet. The choice ultimately came down to the size of the collider, if they had went with Texas’s
magnet, the loop’s diameter would nearly double in size, making the whole thing prohibitively expensive.
But here’s where the drama comes in. The Texas group refused to accept this decision, saying there was no way the R&D team could
meet their deadlines with the other designs. Now whether their design would have been any better, we can’t really say, but they were
right when they predicted that Tigner and his team wouldn’t be able to meet their deadlines. The prototypes were a mess.
Way over budget and behind schedule by over a year. The magnets consistently quenched before achieving the target strength of 6.6 Teslas.
Basically, the fields were so strong that the magnets would literally tear themselves apart if not properly constrained, generating heat that ruined the superconductivity.
Solving this problem took nearly a year of work that ate up much of the R&D budget. In the years since the SSC was first conceived, its estimated cost had ballooned significantly.
In 1982, estimates said $4 billion.
By 84, $8 billion. By 85, $10.7 billion. Now by 88, numbers as high as $14.1 billion were being thrown around.
It had doubled in cost since the DOE first approved the project, all while the federal deficit had been growing wildly out of control.
Congress was instituting tougher and tougher budget restrictions, and if they wanted construction funds, congress was going to have to approve them.
To stave off any cuts, Energy Secretary John Herrington made a vague promise that nearly 30-50% of project funding would come from foreign partners.
But as of yet there had been no eager volunteers. Weird that other countries aren’t so keen to sign on to a project marketed as an America-first
project with American leadership on American soil. I’m sure this definitely isn’t an omen of things to come.
So in the meantime, with no foreign partners, congress denied funding to begin construction for two back to back years, instead only giving out $230 million for more R&D.
The budget was growing, just not as much as the physicists would’ve liked. Construction would have to wait for whoever the next president was going to be.
Behind the scenes, the project had just narrowly avoided a disaster that could have stalled its momentum for years.
The SSC hit its first major budget snag in Spring 1988. Somehow, in a shockingly negligent oversight, the DOE had forgotten to request funding for
the location-search task force. During their travels across the country the task force had racked up a bill of $19 million,
which wasn’t accounted for in the fiscal budget. And Tigner’s boss, Wilmot Hess, who was in charge of the search committee, refused
to go back to congress and request more. Instead, he was insistent that the $19 million be cut from the R&D team’s $61 million,
which put Maury Tigner in one of the worst positions imaginable. It was already halfway through the fiscal year which meant that R&D had already committed
funds to the magnet development, the purchasing of superconducting wire, and staff salaries.
Guess which one the DOE wanted Tigner to cut. And when I mean cut, I actually mean lay off the majority of Tigner’s staff.
Tigner as you might expect, refused to do that, since they were already behind schedule, but also because he’d be laying people off who had no jobs to go back to.
Many of his employees had left comfy university positions to come work for him. Applying for funding for academic jobs is often a months long process with no guarantee
you’ll be approved. If he let them go, he'd be screwing them over, with no guarantee they’d even want to rejoin
the project a full year later. Tensions reached their peak on a particularly nasty Friday the 13th.
Wilmot Hess phoned him up and ordered him to deliver a list of names to fire that same
day. Tigner reluctantly began making a list. Disaster was thankfully averted by lunch, when news came that the chairman of the appropriations
committee had finally allowed DOE to take the missing $19 million from elsewhere. Tigner held his ground, and saved his employees, and likely a ton of momentum for the project.
It was a small victory. But Tigner’s refusal to give into DOE orders had made him some enemies.
When he first joined the project, he was viewed as a highly respected and competent academic. Now, he was labelled as someone who didn't follow orders, and that would have consequences
in the coming months.
Out of the blue, the DOE would receive an unsolicited proposal written by an Edwin Goldwasser, a high ranking member of the R&D team.
